main.summary: At thirty-two Pan Yue saw his first white hairs. On night duty in the palace he began to long for a life in retirement. Starting from the scenes of autumn, the rhapsody voices sorrow at the season, sighs over age and fears the dangers of an official career, and ends with the freedom of farming and wandering among hills and waters.
main.translation:
In the fourteenth year of Jin, I was thirty-two years of spring and autumn, and for the first time saw two-coloured hair. As an aide to the Grand Commandant, concurrently Colonel of the Tiger Guards, I was lodging on night duty in the Office of the Mounted Attendants. Its high pavilions join the clouds and the rays of the sun seldom shine in; those who wear cicada caps and clothe themselves in fine silks and gauze pass their days here. I am a rustic: my resting never went beyond a thatched hut under thick woods, and my talk never beyond guests who were farmers and old men of the fields. Holding office as a stopgap, I have wrongly joined the ranks of the court, rising early and sleeping late, with no leisure to be at ease. I am like a fish in a pond or a bird in a cage, longing for the rivers, lakes, hills and marshes. So I took up the brush and paper and, sighing, wrote this rhapsody. It was autumn then, so I named it after autumn moods. It runs:

The four seasons suddenly change their order, and the ten thousand things whirl and turn back. I look at the time when flowers and plants grow, and see what flourishing and decay depend on. I am moved that winter withers and spring spreads, and sigh that summer is lush and autumn falls. Even the glory and the withering of a humble man belong to the good and bad of human feeling. How well Song Yu said: "How sad is the air of autumn! Desolate, the plants and trees shake and fall, and change into decline. Chilled and shivering, as if on a long journey, climbing a hill and facing the water to see off one who is going home." To see off one who is going home brings a vain longing for companions; the traveller far away feels the bitterness of the wanderer. Facing the river, moved by its flowing, one sighs that time passes; climbing the hills, one longs for the distant and mourns the near. Those four griefs that sicken the heart: to meet even one of them on the road is hard to bear. Alas, autumn days are sad; truly there is no sorrow that does not come to its full.

In the fields the swallows go home; in the damp lowlands the hawks soar. Drifting vapours rise in the morning, withered leaves fall in the evening. So I put away the light fan and laid aside the fine linen. I spread rush mats and put on lined clothes. The garden trees rustle and shed their leaves; a strong wind turns and blows the curtains. The cicada shrills and chants in the cold; the wild geese drift south. The sky is bright and ever higher; the sun is far and slowly fades. How short is the daylight of the faint sun, and I feel the cool night has only begun to lengthen. The moon, hazy, holds its light; the dew, chill and clear, freezes cold. Fireflies glitter at the steps and doors; crickets chirp by the window and screen. I listen to a parted wild goose crying at dawn, and gaze at the last glow of the Fire star as it sinks. At night, uneasy, I cannot sleep, and toss alone in the splendid office. I realise that the year is running out, and with a sigh bow my head and examine myself. Mottled temples hang long under my cap, white hairs rustle down on my collar.

I look up at the free paths of the eminent crowd, who climb the Milky Way and roam. They mount the Spring Terrace in its gladness, with gold and sable gleaming at their ears. If going and staying take different roads, how can I tell the restless from the still? I hear of the fine manner of the perfect man, who makes heaven and earth one in a single finger. Those who know safety forget danger, and so go out of life and into death. In walking, I should put my toes only where a footprint will hold them; yet almost without treading, one reaches the bottom. Where only the edge of a foot can rest, above the springs below, even monkeys and apes would not step. The tortoise, honoured with its bones in the ancestral temple, longs to turn back to the green water.

So I shall gather my robes and go home, and at once throw down my sash and rise high. I shall plough the rich soil of the eastern bank, and pay the small tax in millet. Springs will gush over the rocks, and chrysanthemums spread their scent on the cliff edge. I shall wash in the trickling autumn water and watch the darting minnows splash. I shall wander free in the folds of the hills and rivers, and roam at large in the world of men. Easy and content, I shall pass my years.

keyLines.line: 晉十有四年，余春秋三十有二，始見二毛
keyLines.en: In the fourteenth year of Jin, I was thirty-two years of spring and autumn, and for the first time saw two-coloured hair.
keyLines.note: The preface gives his age and the reason for writing: the first white hairs bring on the feeling of time passing.

keyLines.line: 譬猶池魚籠鳥，有江湖山藪之思
keyLines.en: I am like a pond fish or caged bird, longing for the rivers, lakes, hills and marshes.
keyLines.note: He compares himself to a fish in a pond and a bird in a cage, longing for freedom in nature while serving at court.

keyLines.line: 悲哉秋之為氣也！蕭瑟兮草木搖落而變衰
keyLines.en: How sad is the air of autumn! Desolate, the plants and trees shake and fall, and change into decline.
keyLines.note: It quotes Song Yu's Jiu bian, the source of the tradition of grieving at autumn, and sets the key for the whole rhapsody.

keyLines.line: 庭樹槭以灑落兮，勁風戾而吹帷。蟬嘒嘒而寒吟兮，鴈飄飄而南飛
keyLines.en: The garden trees rustle and fall, a strong wind turns and blows the curtains. The cicada shrills and chants in the cold, the wild geese drift south.
keyLines.note: He lays out the autumn scene in the courtyard, with sound and colour together, building a bleak mood.

keyLines.line: 宵耿介而不寐兮，獨展轉於華省
keyLines.en: At night, uneasy, I cannot sleep, and toss alone in the splendid office.
keyLines.note: He lies awake at night, turning and tossing; the scene turns to feeling.

keyLines.line: 斑鬢髟以承弁兮，素髮颯以垂領
keyLines.en: Mottled temples hang long under my cap, white hairs rustle down on my collar.
keyLines.note: He describes his greying hair directly, and sighs at the passing of his years.

keyLines.line: 彼知安而忘危兮，故出生而入死
keyLines.en: They know safety yet forget danger, and so go out of life and into death.
keyLines.note: He sees that those in high positions know only comfort and forget danger, and so end in deadly trouble, which shows his fear of an official career.

keyLines.line: 逍遙乎山川之阿，放曠乎人間之世。優哉游哉，聊以卒歲
keyLines.en: I will wander free in the folds of the hills and rivers, and roam at large in the world of men. Easy and content, I shall pass my years.
keyLines.note: The ending states his wish to retire; his mood turns from sorrow to openness, in a light tone.

glossary.note: Hair of black mixed with white; it means the first grey hairs.

glossary.en: San ji zhi sheng - the Attendant Cavalier office
glossary.note: The Office of Attendant Cavalier, a government office where Pan Yue was on night duty.

glossary.en: Hu ben zhong lang jiang - Colonel of the Tiger Guards
glossary.note: A military title, in charge of guard duty and attendance on the emperor.

glossary.en: she guan cheng fa - holding a post by filling a gap
glossary.note: To hold an office for a time, filling a vacancy; a modest expression.
A poet of the Chu rhapsody in the Warring States period, who wrote the Jiu bian and began the tradition of sorrow at autumn.
A noble and important government office; here, the Attendant Cavalier office.

glossary.en: er jin diao - gold and sable ornaments
glossary.note: A cap decorated with gold and sable tails; it means a high-ranking official.

glossary.en: tou fu - to throw down the sash
glossary.note: To take off the seal ribbon, meaning to resign from office.

main.background: Pan Yue (247-300) was a writer of the Western Jin who is known for his rhapsodies and elegies. He wrote the Rhapsody on Autumn Moods at thirty-two, while serving as a clerk in the office of the Grand Commandant and as Colonel of the Tiger Guards. It is a leading example of the Wei-Jin rhapsody of sorrow at autumn, and it affected later writing on the theme of autumn moods.
